pr_title: Don't force DRBG reseed on parent reseed
pr_body:
The existing code forces all child DRBGs to reseed if their parent reseeds.  This means that a prediction resistant request (which reseeds the chain up to the primary DRBG) causes all public and private DRBGs to also reseed which is very inefficient (these two exist per thread after all).

This change avoids the forced reseed on parent reseed.  DRBGs will still reseed based on usage and time.

Fixes #20414

- [x] documentation is added or updated
- [x] tests are added or updated
pr_comments: Should we deprecate functions like RAND_add(), RAND_seed() and RAND_poll()?

> Should we deprecate functions like RAND_add(), RAND_seed() and RAND_poll()?

If you want to break pretty much every application that is out there then sure :-)
Any discussion about breaking those APIs belongs elsewhere IMHO and doesn't really related to the DRBG internal handling here in this PR.

> Should we deprecate functions like RAND_add(), RAND_seed() and RAND_poll()?

I don't think so.  These are actually a higher level API than EVP_RAND.

I could envisage them doing nothing however.

> > Should we deprecate functions like RAND_add(), RAND_seed() and RAND_poll()?
> 
> I don't think so. These are actually a higher level API than EVP_RAND.
> 
> I could envisage them doing nothing however.

`RAND_poll()` has already been deprecated in 3.0

`RAND_add()` is still needed IIUC on platforms where automatic seeding from the os is disabled, e.g., due to lack of proper random apis and/or entropy sources. There it is the traditional way for the application to provide some (true or snake oil) randomness.

Does the reseed apply to HRNG sources? I do not recall any requirement to do that for the `_rdrand64` instruction, although there is an associated seed function that is not in the OpenSSL code that I can find.
All seed sources are exempt from reseeding.  This would include the HW source.

> All seed sources are exempt from reseeding. This would include the HW source.

Thanks.

My expectation is that if you call RAND_add(), it will have an
effect on the next RAND_bytes() call, similar to the effect
of requesting the prediction resistance. If that is no longer
the case, it needs to be documented, and I think it's not a bug.

It would be possible to make RAND_bytes() work like you want for the current thread not globally.

Globally, as it is now, is overkill IMO, that could be a lot of DRBGs being reseeded: two per thread in fact.

I have documented the new behaviour.

~OTC: **Do we want this?  If so, is it a bug or a feature?**~

Revised question below.  This approach is wrong, so it's not a question of this being used.
Isn't removing a parameter for reseed counter a separate breaking change?
Not really.  The missing parameter is meaningless and an application can still attempt to fetch it, it just won't return anything.  I could have returned a fixed value instead I guess.

I would expect the RAND_add() to add the entropy to the primary RNG and force reseed of all the child RNGs on next RAND_bytes() call. IMO that is the only reasonable behavior in case there is no proper implicit seed source. On the other hand if the reseed of the primary RNG happens because it was forced by a prediction resistance request on some child RNG, there is no reason why the unrelated children should be forcibly reseeded. So proper solution would IMO be to distinguish these two cases.

Also I would not bother backporting these changes to 3.0 and 3.1.

Shouldn't the removal of the param be mentioned in the docs?

**msp@office:~/src/openssl/master$ git grep -n reseed_count**

[doc/man3/EVP_RAND.pod:314:](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/2c5dbf156f/doc/man3/EVP_RAND.pod#L314) =item "reseed_counter" (B<OSSL_DRBG_PARAM_RESEED_COUNTER>) <unsigned integer>
[doc/man7/EVP_RAND-CTR-DRBG.pod:45:](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/2c5dbf156f/doc/man7/EVP_RAND-CTR-DRBG.pod#L45) =item "reseed_counter" (B<OSSL_DRBG_PARAM_RESEED_COUNTER>) <unsigned integer>
[doc/man7/EVP_RAND-HASH-DRBG.pod:45:](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/2c5dbf156f/doc/man7/EVP_RAND-HASH-DRBG.pod#L45) =item "reseed_counter" (B<OSSL_DRBG_PARAM_RESEED_COUNTER>) <unsigned integer>
[doc/man7/EVP_RAND-HMAC-DRBG.pod:45:](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/2c5dbf156f/doc/man7/EVP_RAND-HMAC-DRBG.pod#L45) =item "reseed_counter" (B<OSSL_DRBG_PARAM_RESEED_COUNTER>) <unsigned integer>
[doc/man7/EVP_RAND-TEST-RAND.pod:47:](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/2c5dbf156f/doc/man7/EVP_RAND-TEST-RAND.pod#L47) =item "reseed_counter" (B<OSSL_DRBG_PARAM_RESEED_COUNTER>) <unsigned integer>
[doc/man7/provider-rand.pod:238:](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/2c5dbf156f/doc/man7/provider-rand.pod#L238) =item "reseed_counter" (B<OSSL_DRBG_PARAM_RESEED_COUNTER>) <unsigned integer>
[include/openssl/core_names.h:268:](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/2c5dbf156f/include/openssl/core_names.h#L268) #define OSSL_DRBG_PARAM_RESEED_COUNTER          "reseed_counter"

Remark: the grep hits in drbg_hash can be ignored.  Unfortunately. the term 'reseed counter' is used in the NIST docs for what we call a 'generate counter'  (You can blame me, I renamed it because it was an annoying name collision.)

[providers/implementations/rands/drbg_hash.c:329:](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/2c5dbf156f/providers/implementations/rands/drbg_hash.c#L329)     int reseed_counter = drbg->generate_counter;
[providers/implementations/rands/drbg_hash.c:331:](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/2c5dbf156f/providers/implementations/rands/drbg_hash.c#L331)     counter[0] = (unsigned char)((reseed_counter >> 24) & 0xff);
[providers/implementations/rands/drbg_hash.c:332:](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/2c5dbf156f/providers/implementations/rands/drbg_hash.c#L332)     counter[1] = (unsigned char)((reseed_counter >> 16) & 0xff);
[providers/implementations/rands/drbg_hash.c:333:](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/2c5dbf156f/providers/implementations/rands/drbg_hash.c#L333)     counter[2] = (unsigned char)((reseed_counter >> 8) & 0xff);
[providers/implementations/rands/drbg_hash.c:334:](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/2c5dbf156f/providers/implementations/rands/drbg_hash.c#L334)     counter[3] = (unsigned char)(reseed_counter & 0xff);
[providers/implementations/rands/drbg_hash.c:345:](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/2c5dbf156f/providers/implementations/rands/drbg_hash.c#L345)            /* (Step 5) V = (V + H + C + reseed_counter) mod (2^seedlen_bits) */
[providers/implementations/rands/drbg_hash.c:348:](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/2c5dbf156f/providers/implementations/rands/drbg_hash.c#L348)            /* V = (V + reseed_counter) mod (2^seedlen_bits) */
[providers/implementations/rands/drbg_local.h:131:](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/2c5dbf156f/providers/implementations/rands/drbg_local.h#L131)      * (Starts at 1). This value is the reseed_counter as defined in

We can't remove the define for this one, that breaks compatibility although I rather doubt anyone uses or cares about this apart from us -- it's used internally to fetch the parent's counter.

The documentation should be updated to say obsolete or the sections removed.

Given [@t8m's comment](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/20437#issuecomment-1456742796), I suspect that's the way forwards.  As for how to implement it, that's another question.

> I would expect the RAND_add() to add the entropy to the primary RNG and force reseed of all the child RNGs on next RAND_bytes() call.

Since the the DRBG instance is owned by the current thread anyway, `RAND_add()` could just set a `need_reseed` flag in the DRBG instance (without any locking) in order to restore the expected behaviour. It wouldn't even require a separate flag, just set the generate counter of the `<public>` DRBG to the reseed threshold
```
    drbg->generate_counter=drbg->reseed_interval
```
after reseeding the `<primary>` DRBG. Then the `<public>` DRBG will reseed automatically on the next call.  (same holds for the `<private>` DRBG of course.)

That gets the thread calling RAND_add reseeded, what about all the other threads?
Reseeding the current thread's public and private instances is easier as part of RAND_add by calling the appropriate reseed functions.

The fundamental issue here is the other threads.  Should they be reseeded after any call to RAND_add?

> That gets the thread calling RAND_add reseeded, what about all the other threads?

The other threads will pick it up in time when they choose to do it. This is not as bad as it sounds. Even with the previous reseed propagation you would not have absolute certainty that all other threads which you are racing against pick your seed up in time before doing some important private operation. It's their job to reseed if necessary.

So why care? To seed all threads with absolute certainty, you need to call `RAND_add()` at application startup, before you create them. Later on, when you have multiple threads, all you can expect is that the _current_ thread picks up the randomness immediately. The other threads need to take care of themselves.

> The fundamental issue here is the other threads. Should they be reseeded after any call to RAND_add?

Your question, reformulated, is: "do we want (downward) seed propagation?"  And the answer is: it would be nice-to-have, but it plays terribly together with (upward) propagation of prediction resistance requests. That's why we removed it. ;-)

But you _did_ know that all other threads would have recently reseeded.  You don't with the proposed change.

Should be an interesting OTC discussion.
I'd rather run my bulldozer over the prediction resistance requests than over the seed propagation.

FIPS mandates prediction resistance reseeds all the way up the chain.  Can't avoid that unfortunately.

PS: I didn't play with the bulldozer.

> But you _did_ know that all other threads would have recently reseeded.  You don't with the proposed change.

There would a much easier way to achieve this: keep the reseed_propation an set the `reseed_interval` and the `reseed_time_interval` to a _very low_ interval, much lower than NIST requires. Say, 1024 generate requests and 5 minutes for all instances. (Note that due to chaining, it will be 1024² requests between reseedings for the primary DRBG). I can't image why this wouldn't be sufficiently secure in practice. And the application wouldn't have to worry about anything.  Shrug.  That's my point of view, but I'm not a researcher, of course.

> FIPS mandates prediction resistance reseeds all the way up the chain. Can't avoid that unfortunately.

I know.  Things still wouldn't be so bad if prediction resistance requests would be an exceptional case (e.g. for generating a long term key) as it used to be, and not as it seems to be know, namely that every ordinary reseed of any of the DRBG instances needs to propagate all the way up to the kernel, making chaining an expensive and useless feature.

OpenSSL doesn't choose prediction resistance anywhere.  Lots of users seem to because _it's more secure_ rather than being required.

My thought is to not count reseeds for prediction resistance in the counters.  I think it's workable.

OTC questions:

**Do we want to do something about the reseed of everything when any DRBG has prediction resistance requested?**

**Do we consider this problem to be a bug and suitable for backport to 3.0 and 3.1?**

Proposal: document that using prediction resistance in a threaded application isn't good and then drop this PR.

Getting the behaviour required looks to be rather invasive.
OTC: document the performance impact of overusing prediction resistance.  Don't worry about fixing the reseeding issue.
See #20452 for resolution

issue_context.title: What is the reason for this code?
issue_context.body:
https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/d0a3b9d1eb1fc510ec3447b44803bbf5520a0c47/providers/implementations/rands/drbg.c#L661-L663

Why the parent DRBG reseeding is to enforce reseeding all the childs?
comments: I'd say to make the entropy newly added to parent to flow down to the child drbgs.
Is it necessary or just useful?

Also, isn't this a performance hog as soon as one of the DRBGs is used with prediction resistance?

If I use `EVP_RAND_generate(RAND_get0_public(), ..., prediction_resistance=1, ...)`, that will cause `ossl_prov_drbg_reseed()` to be called with `prediction_resistance` set to 1. `ossl_prov_drbg_reseed()` will invoke `get_entropy()`, which will call `ossl_drbg_get_seed()`, all with prediction resistance enabled. As I understand things, this will cause all DRBGs on the chain to the top to reseed.

The piece of code quoted in the 1st comment will then cause all other DRBGs to reseed from their parents, which means a single EVP_RAND_generate() with prediction resistance will cause all DRBGs to reseed. In other words, a single EVP_RAND_generate() with prediction resistance will cause all DRBGs to be slow.

What am I missing?

It's useful.  We could technically live without it.  @mspncp introduced this in 1.1.1 I believe, he might be able to supply the reasoning behind this.

_"all other DRBGs"_ is a misnomer, it should be _"the other DRBG"_.  With the setup OpenSSL has by default (primary, public and private), using prediction resistance will cause one unneeded reseed (if you use the public DRBG with prediction resistance, the private DRBG will reseed when next used).  The performance cost won't be huge in reality.

If you are setting up lots of your own DRBGs and using prediction resistance, things might be different.  I'd suggest picking their seed sources carefully or not using prediction resistance.

> _"all other DRBGs"_ is a misnomer, it should be _"the other DRBG"_. With the setup OpenSSL has by default (primary, public and private), using prediction resistance will cause one unneeded reseed (if you use the public DRBG with prediction resistance, the private DRBG will reseed when next used). The performance cost won't be huge in reality.

I had the impression that the public and private DRBGs existed per thread, while the primary DRBG exists once, so it's not just "the other DRBG" if you create threads. Let's assume some application creates 100 threads to handle various different SSL_CTXs, and then creates one additional thread where is uses prediction resistance with the public DRBG. Wouldn't those 100 threads then all re-seed?

> If you are setting up lots of your own DRBGs and using prediction resistance, things might be different. I'd suggest picking their seed sources carefully or not using prediction resistance.

This is not obvious from the documentation, and I doubt anyone will know unless they've actually read the code or strace'd a process with many DRBG instances.

The original design of the OpenSSL 1.1.1 DRBG was a major improvement compared to the singleton locked RNG we had in 1.1.0 and before:  every thread has a dedicated thread-local DRBG  (later it was split into two, a private and a public DRBG) which would provide a lock-free **generate** operation. The child (per-thread) DRBGs **reseed** on a regular base (after some data or time threshold was met), using a **generate** operation to optain fresh random input from the parent (singleton) DRBG.

**The original implementation, however, was different in one important way:**  a reseeding of the child DRBG did not automatically trigger a reseeding of the parent DRBG, even if  `prediction_resistance` was required for the child. So it was possible to have a single thread using `prediction_resistance` without affecting the others too much.

> I had the impression that the public and private DRBGs existed per thread, while the primary DRBG exists once

Exactly, and the primary DRBG is the only one who gets 'true' fresh randomness from the operating system, so the line which @beldmit quoted simply ensures that fresh randomness from the operating system propagates downwards as soon as possibe.

https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/d0a3b9d1eb1fc510ec3447b44803bbf5520a0c47/providers/implementations/rands/drbg.c#L661-L663

The behaviour changed in commit eb238134e0a0fb5ac5c8239ade1dfe77a815aba5 where @kroeckx introduced the concept of propagating the `prediction_restance` requests upwards to the parent:

```patch
@@ -435,7 +437,9 @@ int RAND_DRBG_reseed(RAND_DRBG *drbg,
     drbg->state = DRBG_ERROR;
     if (drbg->get_entropy != NULL)
         entropylen = drbg->get_entropy(drbg, &entropy, drbg->strength,
-                                   drbg->min_entropylen, drbg->max_entropylen);
+                                       drbg->min_entropylen,
+                                       drbg->max_entropylen,
+                                       prediction_resistance);
```

I was strongly opposed to this change, because I believed that the NIST standard does not mandate it, but I was overruled. Maybe I was wrong at the time, or maybe the requirements have become stricter, I don't know. I still dislike this change. You can read the discussion in https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/5402#issuecomment-369513189 ff.

A consequence of this change is that a single thread can trigger an avalanche of reseedings if it overuses the `prediction_resistance` flag, just as @neverpanic describes in https://github.com/openssl/openssl/issues/20414#issuecomment-1450324003.

> Also, isn't this a performance hog as soon as one of the DRBGs is used with prediction resistance?

You are absolutely right.

> Maybe I was wrong at the time, or maybe the requirements have become stricter

It seems like SP 800 90C was more explicit in its requirements https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/5402#issuecomment-370191205

![grafik](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11467854/222451494-96d3606f-405d-4c20-b6eb-651fccb2d9c9.png)

If upward propagation of prediction resistance is mandatory, then one could think of removing the downward propagation of reseedings in favor of smalll reseeding threshholds for the child DRBGs, to break the vicious circle.

But note that currently the downward propagation is crucial for to ensure that the pre-1.1.1 pattern of calling `RAND_add()` before `RAND_bytes()` still works as expected: namely, that the second call will use the 'entropy' provided by the first. That's because `RAND_add()` reseeds the primary DRBG but `RAND_bytes()` uses the per-thread DRBG.

So if you wan't to remove downward propagation, you need to explicitly trigger a reseeding of the thread-local DRBG in `RAND_add()`, in order not to break the behaviour.

I am somewhat concerned, with #20394, that this may be bypassing the hardware RNG in some circumstances. The `get_hardware_random_value()` method does not appear to be invoked even when `--with-rand-seed=rdcpu` is used.

@mspncp we were told by our labthat we need to reseed because of the DRBG chaining and SP 800-90C, and that introduces an endless reseed loop. Now we are trying to get rid of this loop with reasonable modifications.

@beldmit I'm not sure I completely understand what you mean with "we need to reseed": 

Are you saying that all your thread-local DRBGs are configured to request prediction resistance on every generate call?!  Then I understand why you get an infinite loop. If that's the case, the chaining to the primary DRBG is not only completely pointless, but becomes a real bottleneck. I'd suggested that you dump the  primary DRBG and have all thread-local DRBGs reseed using entropy directly from the operating system instead.

> I am somewhat concerned, with #20394, that this may be bypassing the hardware RNG in some circumstances. The `get_hardware_random_value()` method does not appear to be invoked even when `--with-rand-seed=rdcpu` is used.

Sorry, I don't see how these two issues are related?

> > I am somewhat concerned, with #20394, that this may be bypassing the hardware RNG in some circumstances. The `get_hardware_random_value()` method does not appear to be invoked even when `--with-rand-seed=rdcpu` is used.
> 
> Sorry, I don't see how these two issues are related?

I'm just looking for possible causes of why the x86 RNG is not being used on the NonStop platform.

> Are you saying that all your thread-local DRBGs are configured to request prediction resistance on every generate call?! Then I understand why you get an infinite loop. If that's the case, the chaining to the primary DRBG is not only completely pointless, but becomes a real bottleneck. I'd suggested that you dump the primary DRBG and have all thread-local DRBGs reseed using entropy directly from the operating system instead.

No. If we are reseeding the private/public DRBG, we have to reseed the primary first.

> I'm just looking for possible causes of why the x86 RNG is not being used on the NonStop platform.

This issue is just about chaining of DRBGs, i.e., how one DRBG reseeds from another. Your problem concerns the reseeding of the primary DRBG from the operating system, and the answer to your question lies probably hidden somewhere in [rand_unix.c](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/master/providers/implementations/rands/seeding/rand_unix.c).

> No. If we are reseeding the private/public DRBG, we have to reseed the primary first.

That's exactly what `EVP_RAND_generate()` does when you call it with `prediction_resistance = 1`:

- reseed the primary DRBG
- reseed the thread-local private/public DRBG
- generate random data

Oops, I'd forgotten about the per-thread DRBGs.  Yes, there could be a lot of reseeding.

Prediction resistance has to propagate up to the primary, it's a NIST mandate.
I'm not aware of any of our code (outside of tests) setting prediction resistance but an application could do this via the EVP_RAND API.

Given that we do not rely on what is supplied via `RAND_add()`, we could drop the reseed after the parent reseeds.

> Oops, I'd forgotten about the per-thread DRBGs. Yes, there could be a lot of reseeding.
> 
> Prediction resistance has to propagate up to the primary, it's a NIST mandate. I'm not aware of any of our code (outside of tests) setting prediction resistance but an application could do this via the EVP_RAND API.
> 
> Given that we do not rely on what is supplied via `RAND_add()`, we could drop the reseed after the parent reseeds.

In this situation, git is not built with threads - it will soon, but I have not gotten to that particular enhancement on NonStop, and we would have to deal with that when we come to it - git does not do that right now, so it may be an issue there. The only `RAND_` call used by git (checked the object) is `RAND_bytes`.

> > I'm just looking for possible causes of why the x86 RNG is not being used on the NonStop platform.
> 
> This issue is just about chaining of DRBGs, i.e., how one DRBG reseeds from another. Your problem concerns the reseeding of the primary DRBG from the operating system, and the answer to your question lies probably hidden somewhere in [rand_unix.c](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/master/providers/implementations/rands/seeding/rand_unix.c).

I have gone into `rand_unix.c` (seen above in the ifdef/elif/endif block). There is no explicit reference to NonStop compiler defines in that code - I am guessing there needs to be, but I do not get the specific change required.

It's a public patch :)

And reseeding is required by NIST after some amount of operations (65536?). Chain reseeding is also a NIST requirement.

> It's a public patch :)

https://gitlab.com/redhat/centos-stream/rpms/openssl/-/blob/c9s/0076-FIPS-140-3-DRBG.patch, so save everybody some time.

> And reseeding is required by NIST after some amount of operations (65536?).

AFAIK, NIST would be fine with a much larger number of draws before it requires a reseed (something in the range of 2^48), and does not require reseeding after a certain amount of time at all.

> Chain reseeding is also a NIST requirement.

Correct, we've been told by our certification lab that chaining DRBGs is only ok under SP 800-90C if a reseed of the child DRBG reseeds the parent DRBG before using its output as seed, and if that parent DRBG is also used to directly generate random numbers (i.e., is accessible to the user), we also need to reseed it *after* obtaining the seed for the child DRBG, plus this operation must be under a lock so that no user can obtain any information about the state of the DRBG when it was used to seed the child DRBG.

This obviously brings us to the question whether we shouldn't just completely drop DRBG chaining and always seed every DRBG from the kernel instead, since that's more or less what's happening (with a few DRBGs doing some mixing in between).

Note that in the interpretation of our lab, the OpenSSL primary DRBG is also chained to the kernel DRBG, which is why we re-purpose the unused getrandom(GRND_RANDOM) flag to trigger this same reseed dance for the kernel DRBG.
@neverpanic just 2c - I'm not sure GRND_RANDOM is upstream flag.

> @neverpanic just 2c - I'm not sure GRND_RANDOM is upstream flag.

It used to be. It is now unused.

> This obviously brings us to the question whether we shouldn't just completely drop DRBG chaining and always seed every DRBG from the kernel instead, since that's more or less what's happening (with a few DRBGs doing some mixing in between).

That was also my spontaneous suggestion to @beldmit. The sole purpose of the primary DRBG was to avoid a system call on every reseed, which has become futile.

> It's a public patch :)

The _private_ adjective only referred to our discussion, not to the patch 😉

> This obviously brings us to the question whether we shouldn't just completely drop DRBG chaining and always seed every DRBG from the kernel instead, since that's more or less what's happening (with a few DRBGs doing some mixing in between).

Maybe not from the kernel, but what is set up as source of what is now the primary DRBG.

> Correct, we've been told by our certification lab that chaining DRBGs is only ok under SP 800-90C if a reseed of the child DRBG reseeds the parent DRBG before using its output as seed, and if that parent DRBG is also used to directly generate random numbers (i.e., is accessible to the user), we also need to reseed it _after_ obtaining the seed for the child DRBG, plus this operation must be under a lock so that no user can obtain any information about the state of the DRBG when it was used to seed the child DRBG.

I'd be pushing back, if necessary ask for NIST's take on it (as a last resort).  This interpretation is crazy IMO.  It makes chained DRBGs pointless.  Nowhere else is there any discussion of locking, so that's silly too, again IMO.

> I'd be pushing back, if necessary ask for NIST's take on it (as a last resort). This interpretation is crazy IMO. It makes chained DRBGs pointless. Nowhere else is there any discussion of locking, so that's silly too, again IMO.

Following up on this, see FIPS 140-3 IG section D.K, comment 5. Emphasis mine:

There are additional considerations when the stateful conditioning component is a DRBG. For every request to GetEntropy from the entropy source, at least $n_{in}$ bits must be provided to the stateful conditioning component (where $n_{in}$ is defined for the conditioning component and provides $h_{in}$ bits of entropy). If the conditioning component is a DRBG, the conditioning component **shall have prediction resistance enabled, or shall be reseeded** before requesting an output using at least $n_{in}$ bits from the noise source or the previous conditioning component. A stateful conditioning component shall not output any bits without obtaining at least $n_{in}$ bits from the primary noise source or the previous conditioning component. A DRBG is not a bijective conditioning function. The length of the output of the DRBG shall be at most equal to the security strength of the DRBG. **If the DRBG is used in other contexts** than as a conditioning component for the entropy source, **the DRBG shall be reseeded both before and after bits are requested in the other context**. This may occur when one DRBG instance has been instantiated to serve multiple applications such as within an operating system.

This IG doesn't apply to the OpenSSL FIPS provider because there is no claim of an entropy source that is compliant to SP 800-90B.

It could probably be argued that use for a single application doesn't require a reseed on each generate call (at least for the public and private DRBGs): there is no restriction on the number of bits that can be requested in the other context case.  Likewise, it's not specified to be per generate.

This is crazy nonetheless...

review_comments:
It is not sufficient to remove these three lines only. There was a lot of fuzz in the past about potential data races related to the reseed counter, which resulted in some tricky tsan fixes, e.g. in commit a83dc59afa2e0207180d7218efed19b20d48de95  by @bernd-edlinger (see #7399, #7394).

If the downward propagation of reseedings is not wanted anyore then the entire reseed_counter implemention is obsolete and needs to be removed, including all the magic tsan fixes.
